dedupe_keys.name: hurricane marine debris lessons learned from the 2016 and 2017 hurricane seasons florida

description: This report gathers lessons from clearing hurricane marine debris, including sunken and displaced boats, from Florida's waters after Hurricane Matthew in 2016 and Hurricane Irma in 2017. A consultant for the Florida Department of Environmental Protection interviewed 23 staff from NOAA's Marine Debris Program, state agencies, counties, cities, the Coast Guard, contractors and fishing associations, and sorted more than 200 lessons into ten themes such as advance planning, communication, construction, funding and logistics, each marked as a success or a need for improvement. The provider is the Florida Department of Environmental Protection's Florida Coastal Office, with funding from NOAA's coastal management programme. Coverage is the state of Florida, with emphasis on the Florida Keys: after Matthew more than 78,000 cubic yards of debris were removed from state waters for nearly $15 million, and after Irma more than 2,600 vessels were displaced or damaged, 1,824 of them in the Keys, with more than 250,000 cubic yards removed at an estimated $43 million. The July 2018 report is a free PDF from the department, with no licence stated. Caveats: lessons are drawn from interviews, figures were provisional at the time of the study, and no site-level debris data are released. Simulation uses: quantities and costs for post-hurricane debris removal planning, and coordination roles in waste logistics models. Related records: the EPA I-WASTE tool (platform-epa-i-waste) estimates disaster debris and locates disposal facilities.
